reference.source: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology / Rook's Textbook of Dermatology
clinicalPearls: A sensory neuropathy of the dorsal rami of the thoracic spinal nerves, classically involving the T2-T6 segments
Presents with chronic, often intense localised itch (pruritus) of the upper back, usually just medial to or below the scapula
The itch is frequently accompanied by burning, tingling, or a crawling sensation and by tenderness or hypersensitivity in the same area
A characteristic sign is a well-demarcated, often hyperpigmented patch of skin overlying the affected area, produced by chronic rubbing and scratching
It is a neuropathic itch, so it is typically poorly responsive to topical corticosteroids and antihistamines used for inflammatory itch
Underlying degenerative changes of the thoracic spine are often implicated, compressing or irritating the posterior primary rami as they traverse the paraspinal muscles
Management targets the neuropathic mechanism with agents such as topical capsaicin and neuropathic-pain medications, alongside physiotherapy and addressing any contributing spinal pathology
reference.pathophysiology: Notalgia paraesthetica is attributed to dysfunction of the posterior (dorsal) primary rami of the thoracic spinal nerves, most often at the T2-T6 levels, which supply sensation to the skin of the mid-upper back. These rami take an angulated course through the paraspinal musculature, where they are thought to be vulnerable to compression or irritation, frequently in association with degenerative or postural changes of the thoracic spine. The resulting neuropathy generates a chronic neuropathic itch and dysaesthesia confined to the nerve's cutaneous territory. Persistent scratching and rubbing produce secondary skin changes, notably a localised hyperpigmented lichenified patch, and amyloid may deposit in the chronically traumatised skin. Because the itch is neurogenic rather than inflammatory, conventional anti-itch therapy is largely ineffective.
additionalDifferentials: Brachioradial pruritus and other neuropathic itch syndromes
Thoracic radiculopathy from disc or degenerative disease
Primary dermatological disease (contact dermatitis, tinea, lichen simplex chronicus)
Herpes zoster or post-herpetic neuralgia in a thoracic dermatome
Intraspinal or paraspinal mass irritating the dorsal rami
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition of a well-demarcated pruritic hyperpigmented patch in the T2-T6 distribution
Skin examination to exclude a primary dermatosis
Skin biopsy if amyloid deposition or another dermatosis is suspected
Imaging of the thoracic spine when a compressive or degenerative cause is suspected
Neurological examination to exclude a radiculopathy or myelopathy
Trial of neuropathic therapy as both treatment and supportive confirmation of the mechanism
redFlags: New neurological deficit or band-like sensory level suggesting a spinal cord lesion
A vesicular eruption in the affected dermatome indicating herpes zoster
Rapidly changing or ulcerating skin lesion warranting biopsy for malignancy
Progressive or bilateral symptoms suggesting an underlying structural spinal cause
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign but often chronic and relapsing; symptoms may be controlled with neuropathic therapy and by addressing spinal or postural contributors, though complete and lasting resolution can be difficult to achieve.
pitfalls: Treating it as an inflammatory dermatosis with steroids and antihistamines, which rarely help neuropathic itch
Mistaking the hyperpigmented lichenified patch for a primary skin disease or malignancy
Overlooking associated thoracic spine degeneration that may be driving the neuropathy
Failing to distinguish it from herpes zoster or a thoracic radiculopathy with a genuine sensory level
references: Adams and Victor's Principles of Neurology
